intro:
Vietnamese restaurant phone orders can be handled by an AI phone host that answers the line, takes the order, and sends it to the kitchen. It can also answer hours, address, parking, and menu questions so your staff does not have to stop cooking or serving to pick up the phone.

For an independent pho shop, banh mi counter, or family restaurant, this can be a practical way to keep takeout moving during rushes. ROAL is built for that kind of phone work, and you can set it up from your website or menu in about a minute.

sections.h2: What phone orders look like in a Vietnamese restaurant
sections.body:
Vietnamese menus often have a lot of customization. Callers may want pho with rare steak, extra noodles, no cilantro, or a certain spice level. They may also ask about vermicelli bowls, banh mi fillings, spring rolls, and soups of the day.

That creates a lot of back-and-forth at the counter. A phone host should be able to collect the exact items, sizes, modifiers, and notes, then repeat them back clearly.

A simple phone flow can sound like this:
- "Thanks for calling. What can I get started for pickup today?"
- "Just to confirm, that is one large pho with brisket, no onions, extra basil, and one grilled pork banh mi."
- "Your order will be ready in about 20 minutes."

If you want a Vietnamese restaurant phone orders setup that feels natural, focus on the menu items people ask for most often and make sure the phone host can read them from the live menu.

sections.h2: Which calls should the phone host handle, and which should go to staff?
sections.body:
A good rule is simple: let the phone host handle the routine calls, and send the tricky ones to your team. ROAL can take pickup and delivery orders, answer basic questions about hours, address, parking, and menu items, and take reservation requests.

It should also hand off calls like these with a summary:
- catering requests
- complaints
- allergy-sensitive questions
- manager requests

That matters for Vietnamese restaurants because allergy questions can come up with fish sauce, peanuts, shrimp, soy, and broth ingredients. The phone host should not guess. It should move those calls to staff.

A helpful script for staff handoff is: "I have a caller asking about ingredients in the broth and wants to speak with the manager." That keeps the kitchen focused and gives the caller a clear next step.

If you are comparing phone options, [AI phone host vs answering service](/compare/answering-service) is worth a look, especially if you want order-taking instead of message taking.

sections.body:

You can also upload a menu in any format. Then you test-call it right in the browser before going live, with no sign-up needed.

A practical setup checklist:

sections.h2: What should the phone host say on a real order call?
sections.body:
The best phone flow is short and repeatable. The caller should hear a friendly greeting, give the order, and hear it back clearly before the kitchen gets it.

A useful script pattern for Vietnamese restaurant phone orders is:
- "Thanks for calling. Pickup or delivery?"
- "What name should I put on the order?"
- "Can I repeat that back to make sure it is right?"
- "Your order should be ready at 6:10."

The host should collect the caller’s name and phone number, quote a ready time, and confirm the order back. It should not take card numbers over the phone. Payment happens at pickup or however your restaurant already takes it.

For example, say your average pickup order is $28. If you handle 40 completed phone orders in a month, that is 40 orders x $0.90 = $36 in ROAL usage for completed orders. Plug in your own order count and average size to compare it with delivery app commissions or staffing costs.

sections.h2: How do I keep the phone line working with my current number?
sections.body:
You do not have to give up your restaurant number. When you claim the host, ROAL gives each location its own phone line automatically, and you forward your existing number to it.

You can forward all calls, or only when busy or unanswered. That means the phone can ring normally most of the time, and ROAL can step in when your team is slammed.

A basic call forwarding checklist:
- Confirm your carrier or phone system supports the code you want to use.
- Test forwarding with one real call.
- Make sure the host answers the way you expect.
- Turn forwarding off any time if you want to change it.

For many landlines and some carriers, *72 then the forwarding number forwards all calls, and *73 turns it off. On some GSM mobile carriers, **21*number# forwards all calls and ##21# turns it off; **61*number# forwards unanswered calls and **67*number# forwards busy calls. Verizon Wireless uses *72 / *73, and *71 for busy/no-answer forwarding. Business VoIP systems usually set forwarding in the web portal. Codes vary by carrier and plan, so always confirm with your carrier and test with a call. You can also check [call forwarding codes by carrier](/tools/call-forwarding-codes).

sections.h2: What should I watch after launch so the phone host stays useful?
sections.body:
After launch, keep the menu and hours current. That matters most for restaurants with specials, lunch combos, sold-out items, or seasonal soups.

ROAL includes a dashboard with live kitchen tickets, call history with transcripts and recordings, menu editing, hours, FAQs, upsell suggestions, and multi-location menus. Questions the host could not answer go into an inbox. You answer once, and the host knows it from then on.

A simple weekly check is enough for many owners:
- review missed questions in the inbox
- update sold-out items
- confirm holiday hours
- listen to one or two call recordings
- check that the ready-time quotes still feel right

If you run more than one shop, the same idea can scale across locations. ROAL also supports separate menus and call handling by location, which is useful for groups that share a brand but not the exact same hours or menu.
